items.stem: Which statement about the solubility of salts in water is correct?
items.answer: All nitrates are soluble.
items.markingKey: Solubility rules: all nitrates are soluble; all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble.

items.stem: A student says, "Calcium carbonate is soluble because all calcium compounds dissolve." Explain why this is wrong.
items.answer: Carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium; calcium carbonate is insoluble (e.g. limestone does not dissolve in water).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: carbonate rule; 1 mark: CaCO₃ insoluble [2]

items.stem: Explain why barium sulfate can be prepared by mixing two solutions but zinc sulfate cannot.
items.answer: Barium sulfate is insoluble so it forms as a precipitate that can be filtered off; zinc sulfate is soluble so it stays dissolved with the other product and cannot be separated by filtration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: BaSO₄ insoluble/precipitates; 1 mark: ZnSO₄ soluble, stays in solution [2]

items.stem: Aqueous iron(II) chloride is mixed with aqueous potassium hydroxide. Which substance, if any, forms as a precipitate?
items.answer: iron(II) hydroxide
items.markingKey: Yes: iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₂, precipitates because hydroxides are insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium hydroxides (calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble).

items.stem: Aqueous calcium nitrate is added to aqueous potassium sulfate. Predict whether a precipitate forms. If it does, name it and write the ionic equation, with state symbols.
items.answer: Yes: calcium sulfate, CaSO₄, precipitates because sulfates are soluble except barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates. Ionic equation: Ca²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → CaSO₄(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: precipitate named (calcium sulfate); 1 mark: ionic equation Ca²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → CaSO₄(s); 1 mark: state symbols [3]

items.stem: Tomás reads that lead(II) chloride, PbCl₂, is used in industry and wants to make some in the laboratory. (a) Name the most suitable method of preparation and explain your choice. (b) Explain why the precipitate is washed with distilled water before drying.
items.answer: (a) precipitation (b) To remove the soluble sodium nitrate and any unreacted solution from the surface of the solid.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: precipitation; 1 mark: reason (salt is insoluble) [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which hydroxide is soluble in water?
items.answer: potassium hydroxide
items.markingKey: Hydroxides are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium (calcium hydroxide slightly).

items.stem: Explain why the solubility rules tell you that every nitrate salt can be used as a source of a metal ion in solution.
items.answer: All nitrates are soluble, so a metal nitrate dissolves to give the metal ions in aqueous solution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: all nitrates soluble; 1 mark: provides aqueous cations [2]

items.stem: Mateo predicts that lead(II) chloride, PbCl₂, is soluble in water. Use the solubility rules to explain whether Mateo is correct.
items.answer: Mateo is incorrect: lead(II) chloride is insoluble because chlorides are soluble except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct conclusion (insoluble); 1 mark: rule quoted (chlorides are soluble except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride) [2]

items.stem: A technician has samples of silver nitrate, barium carbonate, iron(III) hydroxide, potassium nitrate, magnesium chloride. Using the solubility rules, sort them into soluble and insoluble compounds.
items.answer: Soluble: silver nitrate, potassium nitrate, magnesium chloride. Insoluble: barium carbonate, iron(III) hydroxide.
items.markingKey: All five correct [3]; four correct [2]; three correct [1].

items.stem: A technician has samples of aluminium chloride, aluminium nitrate, potassium chloride, lead(II) hydroxide, barium chloride. Using the solubility rules, sort them into soluble and insoluble compounds.
items.answer: Soluble: aluminium chloride, aluminium nitrate, potassium chloride, barium chloride. Insoluble: lead(II) hydroxide.
items.markingKey: All five correct [3]; four correct [2]; three correct [1].

items.stem: Why is the insoluble base added in excess when a soluble salt is prepared from an acid?
options: To make sure all the acid reacts
items.answer: To make sure all the acid reacts
items.markingKey: Excess base ensures all the acid is used up; the unreacted solid is then removed by filtration.

items.stem: Explain why the acid is often warmed before the insoluble base is added.
items.answer: The reaction is faster at a higher temperature, so the base dissolves/reacts more quickly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster rate; 1 mark: particles have more energy / more frequent collisions [2]

items.stem: Explain why the excess-solid method cannot be used to make sodium sulfate.
items.answer: Sodium compounds (oxide, hydroxide, carbonate) are soluble, so any excess would dissolve and could not be filtered off; titration is used instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sodium bases soluble; 1 mark: excess cannot be removed by filtration [2]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction between zinc carbonate and nitric acid to make zinc nitrate.
items.answer: ZnCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂
items.markingKey: ZnCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂: 1 mark correct formulae; 1 mark balancing [2]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction between zinc oxide and hydrochloric acid to make zinc chloride. Include state symbols.
items.answer: ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O (states: base (s), acid (aq), salt (aq), water (l), gas (g))
items.markingKey: ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O: 1 mark correct formulae; 1 mark balancing; 1 mark state symbols [3]

items.stem: Elena adds excess iron to 40.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the maximum mass of iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂, that could be obtained.

Nadia prepares crystals of iron(II) chloride using 60.0 cm³ of 1.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and an excess of iron. (a) Calculate the maximum mass of FeCl₂ (Mr = 127) that can form. (b) The percentage yield was 78%. Calculate the mass of crystals obtained and suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) 5.72 g (b) 4.46 g; e.g. some salt remains dissolved in the solution after crystallisation / losses on transfer.

items.stem: Omar prepares crystals of iron(II) chloride using 50.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and an excess of iron(II) carbonate. (a) Calculate the number of moles of hydrochloric acid used. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of FeCl₂ (Mr = 127) that can form. (c) Explain why iron(II) carbonate is suitable for this method but sodium carbonate would not be.
items.answer: (a) 0.100 mol (b) 6.35 g (c) Iron(II) carbonate is insoluble, so the excess can be filtered off; sodium compounds are soluble and would contaminate the solution.

items.stem: Explain why calcium carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid are not used to prepare calcium sulfate crystals.
items.answer: Calcium sulfate is insoluble; it coats the carbonate and the reaction soon stops, and the salt cannot be crystallised from solution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: CaSO₄ insoluble; 1 mark: layer stops reaction / salt not in solution [2]

items.stem: Explain why crystals are dried between filter papers or in a warm oven rather than by strong heating.
items.answer: Strong heating would remove water of crystallisation (or decompose the salt), changing its appearance and composition.

items.stem: A student adds copper(II) oxide to dilute sulfuric acid until no more dissolves and then filters. Describe what is seen in the filter paper and in the filtrate.
items.answer: Black solid (excess copper(II) oxide) in the filter paper; blue solution of copper(II) sulfate as the filtrate.

items.stem: Kenji adds excess zinc to 40.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the maximum mass of zinc chloride, ZnCl₂, that could be obtained.

Chloe adds excess copper(II) oxide to 75.0 cm³ of 0.800 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O. Calculate (i) the maximum mass of copper(II) chloride, CuCl₂, that could be obtained. (ii) The student actually obtains 3.65 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

A teacher in Santiago demonstrates the preparation of zinc nitrate from zinc carbonate and 60.0 cm³ of nitric acid of concentration 1.00 mol/dm³. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (b) Explain why zinc carbonate is suitable for this method but sodium carbonate would not be.
items.answer: (a) ZnCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (b) Zinc carbonate is insoluble, so the excess can be filtered off; sodium compounds are soluble and would contaminate the solution.

items.stem: Lina prepares crystals of iron(II) nitrate using 40.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ nitric acid and an excess of iron(II) carbonate. (a) Calculate the maximum mass of Fe(NO₃)₂ (Mr = 180) that can form. (b) The percentage yield was 85%. Calculate the mass of crystals obtained and suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100%. (c) Explain why iron(II) carbonate is suitable for this method but sodium carbonate would not be.
items.answer: (a) 1.80 g (b) 1.53 g; e.g. some salt remains dissolved in the solution after crystallisation / losses on transfer. (c) Iron(II) carbonate is insoluble, so the excess can be filtered off; sodium compounds are soluble and would contaminate the solution.

items.stem: Which salt is best prepared by titration of an acid with an alkali?
items.answer: potassium nitrate
items.markingKey: Potassium compounds are soluble, so the salt is made by exact neutralisation of KOH with HNO₃.

items.stem: Explain why the titration is repeated with the same volumes but no indicator when making a salt for use.
items.answer: The indicator would contaminate the salt; repeating with the known volumes gives a neutral salt solution with no indicator.

items.stem: Explain why the excess-solid method cannot be used to prepare ammonium sulfate.
items.answer: Ammonia/ammonium compounds are soluble (aqueous ammonia is an alkali), so there is no insoluble excess to filter off; an exact volume must be found by titration.

items.stem: 10.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is titrated with 0.400 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the volume of acid needed to neutralise the alkali.
items.answer: 6.25 cm³

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is titrated with 0.250 mol/dm³ nitric acid. NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the volume of acid needed to neutralise the alkali.
items.answer: 15.0 cm³

items.stem: Sipho titrates 20.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide with 0.120 mol/dm³ nitric acid using methyl orange indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 0.00, final 17.75; titration 1: initial 0.00, final 17.00; titration 2: initial 0.00, final 17.00; titration 3: initial 0.50, final 17.45. (a) Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results. (b) Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide. KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O
items.answer: (a) 16.98 cm³ (b) 0.102 mol/dm³

items.stem: Why is an indicator needed when a soluble salt is made from an acid and an alkali?
options: Both reactants and the product are soluble, so the end-point cannot be seen without one
items.answer: Both reactants and the product are soluble, so the end-point cannot be seen without one
items.markingKey: Nothing visible shows when neutralisation is complete; an indicator changes colour at the end-point.

items.stem: Explain why the conical flask is swirled during a titration.
items.answer: To mix the acid and alkali so that the colour change shows the true end-point.

items.stem: Aqueous ammonia is neutralised by nitric acid. What is the formula of the salt formed?
items.answer: NH₄NO₃

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the neutralisation of potassium hydroxide by sulfuric acid.
items.answer: 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

items.stem: Ines titrates 20.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide with 0.120 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid using thymolphthalein indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 0.80, final 24.70; titration 1: initial 2.35, final 25.45; titration 2: initial 2.35, final 25.50; titration 3: initial 2.35, final 25.45. (a) State the colour change at the end-point. (b) Describe how you would then obtain pure dry crystals of potassium sulfate.
items.answer: (a) blue to colourless (b) Repeat the titration with the same volumes but no indicator; heat the solution to the point of crystallisation; cool; filter and dry crystals.

items.stem: Which pair of solutions could be mixed to prepare insoluble barium sulfate?
items.answer: barium nitrate and sodium sulfate
items.markingKey: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s); both reactants must be soluble.

items.stem: Explain why the precipitate is dried in a warm oven rather than heated strongly.
items.answer: Strong heating might decompose the salt (e.g. carbonates give oxides); a warm oven removes the water without changing the salt.

items.stem: Explain why lead(II) chloride can be made by mixing aqueous lead(II) nitrate with aqueous sodium chloride.
items.answer: Both reactants are soluble (nitrates and sodium salts) so they provide the ions; lead(II) chloride is insoluble so it precipitates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reactants soluble; 1 mark: product insoluble [2]

items.stem: Aqueous barium chloride is mixed with aqueous sodium carbonate. Write (a) the balanced symbol equation and (b) the ionic equation for the reaction.
items.answer: (a) BaCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → BaCO₃ + 2NaCl (b) Ba²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → BaCO₃

items.stem: Aqueous calcium chloride is mixed with aqueous potassium sulfate. Write (a) the balanced symbol equation and (b) the ionic equation for the reaction. Include state symbols.
items.answer: (a) CaCl₂ + K₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + 2KCl (b) Ca²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → CaSO₄ — precipitate (s), others (aq)
items.markingKey: (a) formulae [1], balancing [1]; (b) ionic equation [1]; state symbols [1]

items.stem: Freya prepares lead(II) iodide by mixing 50.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ lead(II) nitrate with an excess of aqueous potassium iodide. (a) State the colour of the precipitate. (b) Describe how a pure dry sample of the salt is obtained from the mixture.
items.answer: (a) bright yellow (b) Filter; wash the residue with distilled water; dry in a warm oven or between filter papers.

items.stem: Explain why barium sulfate cannot be made by adding barium carbonate to dilute sulfuric acid.
items.answer: Insoluble barium sulfate forms a layer on the carbonate, stopping the reaction; also the product would be mixed with unreacted carbonate.

items.stem: Explain the meaning of the term "spectator ion", using the formation of silver chloride as an example.
items.answer: Ions present in the solution that do not take part in the reaction, e.g. Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ when AgNO₃(aq) and NaCl(aq) are mixed.

items.stem: Aqueous calcium nitrate is mixed with aqueous sodium sulfate. Which is the ionic equation for the precipitation?
items.answer: Ca²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → CaSO₄
items.markingKey: Ca²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → CaSO₄; the other ions are spectators.

items.stem: Excess aqueous sodium carbonate is added to 25.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol/dm³ barium nitrate. Ba(NO₃)₂ + Na₂CO₃ → BaCO₃ + 2NaNO₃. Calculate the mass of dry barium carbonate precipitate that forms.

Isla prepares magnesium carbonate by mixing 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ magnesium chloride with an excess of aqueous sodium carbonate. (a) State the colour of the precipitate. (b) Name the soluble by-product that remains in solution. (c) Calculate the maximum mass of precipitate (Mr = 84).
items.answer: (a) white (b) sodium chloride (c) 2.10 g

items.stem: What is meant by water of crystallisation?
options: Water used to dissolve a salt
Water produced when an acid reacts with a base
Water molecules chemically combined in a fixed ratio within a crystalline salt
Water that evaporates from a salt solution
items.answer: Water molecules chemically combined in a fixed ratio within a crystalline salt
items.markingKey: Water of crystallisation: water molecules present in hydrated crystals in a definite proportion.

items.stem: What colour change is seen when blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated strongly?
items.answer: blue to white
items.markingKey: CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) → CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(g): water of crystallisation is driven off.

items.stem: Explain why adding water to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate can be used as a test for water.
items.answer: Water recombines to form blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate; the colour change from white to blue shows water is present.

items.stem: When 3.44 g of hydrated zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄·xH₂O, is heated until all the water is removed, 1.93 g of anhydrous ZnSO₄ remains. Calculate x.

Freya investigates hydrated zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄·xH₂O. A 3.44 g sample is heated in a crucible; its mass is recorded after each heating: 2.61 g, 2.16 g, 1.93 g, 1.93 g. (a) Explain why the sample was heated several times. (b) Calculate the mass of water lost.
items.answer: (a) To make sure all the water of crystallisation was removed — heating to constant mass. (b) 1.51 g

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in hydrated zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄·7H₂O.

Yusuf investigates hydrated sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄·xH₂O. A 3.86 g sample is heated in a crucible; its mass is recorded after each heating: 2.67 g, 2.02 g, 1.70 g, 1.70 g. (a) Calculate the mass of water lost. (b) Calculate the value of x. (c) Suggest why a lid is placed loosely on the crucible.
items.answer: (a) 2.16 g (b) 10 (c) To prevent loss of solid by spitting while allowing water vapour to escape.

items.stem: Which pair of chlorides are both insoluble in water?
items.answer: silver chloride and lead(II) chloride
items.markingKey: Chlorides are soluble except AgCl and PbCl₂.

items.stem: Explain why sodium carbonate solution is used, rather than calcium carbonate, to provide carbonate ions for a precipitation.
items.answer: Sodium carbonate is soluble, so it provides carbonate ions in solution; calcium carbonate is insoluble and provides no free carbonate ions.

items.stem: Aqueous copper(II) chloride is mixed with aqueous sodium carbonate. Which substance, if any, forms as a precipitate?
items.answer: copper(II) carbonate
items.markingKey: Yes: copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃, precipitates because carbonates are insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.

items.stem: Hana reads that iron(II) nitrate, Fe(NO₃)₂, is used in industry and wants to make some in the laboratory. (a) State whether iron(II) nitrate is soluble or insoluble in water. (b) Outline the main steps of the method.
items.answer: (a) soluble (b) add an excess of the insoluble base, carbonate or metal to warm acid, filter off the excess, heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation, cool and dry the crystals
items.markingKey: (a) all nitrates are soluble [1] (b) 1 mark per correct step, up to [3]

items.stem: How is the unreacted excess copper(II) oxide removed from copper(II) sulfate solution?
items.answer: filtration
items.markingKey: The excess solid oxide is insoluble and stays on the filter paper; the filtrate is the salt solution.

items.stem: Explain how you could tell that a sample of the crystals is pure.
items.answer: Pure crystals have a sharp melting point (or, for a hydrate, are uniform in shape and colour); impurities widen and lower the melting range.

items.stem: Yusuf adds excess magnesium carbonate to 75.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. MgCO₃ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the maximum mass of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, that could be obtained.

Calculate the minimum mass of magnesium carbonate, MgCO₃, needed to react completely with 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Suggest why a larger mass is used in practice. (MgCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂)
items.answer: 2.10 g; excess is used so that all the acid reacts and the salt is not contaminated with acid.

items.stem: Nadia prepares crystals of iron(II) sulfate using 60.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid and an excess of iron(II) carbonate. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (b) Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid used.
items.answer: (a) FeCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂ (b) 0.0300 mol

items.stem: Which reagents are titrated together to prepare ammonium sulfate?
items.answer: aqueous ammonia and sulfuric acid

items.stem: Explain why the acid is added drop by drop near the end-point.
items.answer: One drop can change the indicator colour; adding drop by drop prevents overshooting the end-point.

items.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.250 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is titrated with 0.125 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the volume of acid needed to neutralise the alkali.
items.answer: 50.0 cm³

items.stem: Tomás titrates 20.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide with 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid using thymolphthalein indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 1.05, final 18.45; titration 1: initial 0.00, final 17.00; titration 2: initial 0.80, final 17.80; titration 3: initial 0.80, final 17.75. (a) Calculate each titre and identify the concordant results. (b) Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results. (c) State the colour change at the end-point. (d) Suggest one source of error that would make the titre too large.
items.answer: (a) 17.40; 17.00; 17.00; 16.95 cm³; concordant: 17.00, 17.00, 16.95 (b) 16.98 cm³ (c) blue to colourless (d) e.g. air bubble in the burette jet / overshooting the end-point / reading the meniscus from above.
items.markingKey: (a) titre = final − initial for each [1]; concordant = within 0.10 cm³, rough excluded [1]; total [2] (b) mean of 17.00, 17.00, 16.95 [1] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Explain why the filter paper and precipitate are rinsed with a little distilled water rather than tap water.
items.answer: Tap water contains dissolved ions (e.g. Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) that would contaminate the salt or form further precipitate.

items.stem: To prepare silver iodide, Freya kept the filtrate and threw away the residue. Explain the mistake and how to correct it.
items.answer: The silver iodide is the insoluble residue on the filter paper; the filtrate contains only sodium nitrate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: why it is wrong; 1 mark: correction [2]

items.stem: Aqueous silver nitrate is mixed with aqueous sodium bromide. Write (a) the balanced symbol equation and (b) the ionic equation for the reaction.
items.answer: (a) AgNO₃ + NaBr → AgBr + NaNO₃ (b) Ag⁺ + Br⁻ → AgBr

items.stem: In a water-testing laboratory, an insoluble salt, calcium carbonate, is made from 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ calcium chloride and excess sodium carbonate solution. (a) State the colour of the precipitate. (b) Name the soluble by-product that remains in solution. (c) The dry mass obtained was 2.33 g. Calculate the percentage yield and suggest one reason why it is below 100%. (d) Explain why calcium chloride is used rather than calcium hydroxide as the source of calcium ions.
items.answer: (a) white (b) sodium chloride (c) 93.2%; some solid lost on the filter paper or in transfer. (d) Calcium chloride is soluble so it provides free calcium ions; the alternative is insoluble.

items.stem: Explain why the dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate is described as a reversible reaction.
items.answer: Heating removes water to give white anhydrous salt; adding water back reforms the blue hydrated salt.

items.stem: When 5.48 g of hydrated calcium chloride, CaCl₂·xH₂O, is heated until all the water is removed, 2.78 g of anhydrous CaCl₂ remains. Calculate x.

Chloe investigates hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O. A 4.88 g sample is heated in a crucible; its mass is recorded after each heating: 4.48 g, 4.27 g, 4.16 g, 4.16 g. (a) Calculate the mass of water lost. (b) Calculate the value of x.
Which three sulfates are insoluble in water?
options: magnesium sulfate, iron(II) sulfate and barium sulfate
barium sulfate, calcium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate
potassium sulfate, calcium sulfate and ammonium sulfate
sodium sulfate, copper(II) sulfate and zinc sulfate
items.answer: barium sulfate, calcium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate
items.markingKey: Sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead.

items.stem: Distinguish between a soluble and an insoluble salt, giving one example of each.
items.answer: A soluble salt dissolves in water to form a solution (e.g. sodium chloride); an insoluble salt does not dissolve appreciably (e.g. silver chloride).

items.stem: Aqueous lead(II) nitrate is mixed with aqueous potassium carbonate. Which substance, if any, forms as a precipitate?
items.answer: lead(II) carbonate
items.markingKey: Yes: lead(II) carbonate, PbCO₃, precipitates because carbonates are insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.

items.stem: Ines reads that iron(III) nitrate, Fe(NO₃)₃, is used in industry and wants to make some in the laboratory. (a) State whether iron(III) nitrate is soluble or insoluble in water. (b) Outline the main steps of the method.
items.answer: (a) soluble (b) add an excess of the insoluble base, carbonate or metal to warm acid, filter off the excess, heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation, cool and dry the crystals
items.markingKey: (a) all nitrates are soluble [1] (b) 1 mark per correct step, up to [3]

items.stem: Which pair of reagents can be used to make zinc chloride by the excess-solid method?
items.answer: zinc carbonate and hydrochloric acid
items.markingKey: Excess insoluble ZnCO₃ + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

items.stem: Omar tried to make crystals of iron(II) nitrate from iron(II) carbonate and an acid but heated the filtrate of iron(II) nitrate to dryness in an evaporating basin. Explain what is wrong with this step and how it should be corrected.
items.answer: Heating to dryness removes water of crystallisation (and may decompose the salt), giving a powder rather than hydrated crystals. Heat to the point of crystallisation then leave to cool.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the consequence; 1 mark: correct procedure [2]

items.stem: Grace adds excess magnesium hydroxide to 50.0 cm³ of 0.400 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. Mg(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the maximum mass of magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄, that could be obtained.

Calculate the minimum mass of magnesium carbonate, MgCO₃, needed to react completely with 40.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Suggest why a larger mass is used in practice. (MgCO₃ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂)
items.answer: 3.36 g; excess is used so that all the acid reacts and the salt is not contaminated with acid.

items.stem: In a water-testing laboratory, iron(II) chloride is made by adding iron(II) oxide a little at a time to 40.0 cm³ of warm 2.00 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid until it is in excess. (a) Describe how you would know that the solid is in excess. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of FeCl₂ (Mr = 127) that can form.
items.answer: (a) Solid remains undissolved. (b) 5.08 g

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which apparatus measures exactly 25.0 cm³ of alkali into the conical flask? (b) Why is an indicator needed when a soluble salt is made from an acid and an alkali?
items.answer: (a) volumetric pipette (b) Both reactants and the product are soluble, so the end-point cannot be seen without one
items.markingKey: (a) A pipette delivers a fixed volume accurately. (b) Nothing visible shows when neutralisation is complete; an indicator changes colour at the end-point.

items.stem: Ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). Explain why this equation applies to every acid–alkali neutralisation.
items.answer: All acids provide H⁺ ions and all alkalis provide OH⁻ ions; the other ions (spectator ions) do not change, so the net reaction is always H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

items.stem: 10.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is titrated with 0.400 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the volume of acid needed to neutralise the alkali.
items.answer: 3.75 cm³

items.stem: Mei titrates 20.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide with 0.120 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid using methyl orange indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 3.10, final 23.35; titration 1: initial 2.35, final 22.75; titration 2: initial 0.80, final 20.60; titration 3: initial 0.00, final 19.85. (a) Calculate each titre and identify the concordant results. (b) Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results. (c) State the colour change at the end-point. (d) Suggest one source of error that would make the titre too large.
items.answer: (a) 20.25; 20.40; 19.80; 19.85 cm³; concordant: 19.80, 19.85 (b) 19.83 cm³ (c) yellow to orange/red (d) e.g. air bubble in the burette jet / overshooting the end-point / reading the meniscus from above.
items.markingKey: (a) titre = final − initial for each [1]; concordant = within 0.10 cm³, rough excluded [1]; total [2] (b) mean of 19.80, 19.85 [1] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: To prepare calcium sulfate, Grace did not wash the precipitate. Explain the mistake and how to correct it.
items.answer: Soluble sodium nitrate remains on the solid, so it is impure; wash with distilled water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: why it is wrong; 1 mark: correction [2]

items.stem: To prepare lead(II) sulfate, Nadia used solid lead(II) carbonate instead of aqueous lead(II) nitrate. Explain the mistake and how to correct it.
items.answer: The cation must be in solution; an insoluble solid provides no free ions (and would contaminate the product). Use a soluble salt such as the nitrate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: why it is wrong; 1 mark: correction [2]

items.stem: Aqueous zinc chloride is mixed with aqueous sodium carbonate. Write (a) the balanced symbol equation and (b) the ionic equation for the reaction.
items.answer: (a) ZnCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → ZnCO₃ + 2NaCl (b) Zn²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → ZnCO₃

items.stem: Hana prepares barium sulfate by mixing 40.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ barium chloride with an excess of aqueous potassium sulfate. (a) Write the ionic equation, with state symbols. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of precipitate (Mr = 233). (c) The dry mass obtained was 1.68 g. Calculate the percentage yield and suggest one reason why it is below 100%.
items.answer: (a) Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s) (b) 1.86 g (c) 90.3%; some solid lost on the filter paper or in transfer.
items.markingKey: (a) ions (aq) [1]; product (s) and balanced [1]; total [2] (b) n = 40.0/1000 × 0.200 = 0.00800 mol [1]; mass = 1.86 g [1]; total [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Explain why a hydrated salt is heated "to constant mass" when finding the formula of the hydrate.
items.answer: Repeated heating until the mass stops changing ensures all the water of crystallisation has been removed.

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

Sofia investigates hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O. A 3.69 g sample is heated in a crucible; its mass is recorded after each heating: 2.65 g, 2.08 g, 1.80 g, 1.80 g. (a) Explain why the sample was heated several times. (b) Describe a test to show that the vapour given off is water.
items.answer: (a) To make sure all the water of crystallisation was removed — heating to constant mass. (b) Condense it and add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: white → blue (or cobalt(II) chloride paper blue → pink); pure water boils at 100 °C.
